extracted.intended_audience: designers, design owners, IP attorneys/agents and businesses seeking international design protection via the WIPO Hague System
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for filing and managing an international industrial/design registration under the WIPO Hague System, including eligibility, filing formalities, publication, substantive examination, refusals, duration, and post-registration management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to use the Hague System
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file an international application under the Hague System if you: are a national of, have a domicile or habitual residence in, or have a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in any Hague System member (referred to as 'contracting party'), including any country of the European Union (EU) or the African Intellectual Property Organization (OAPI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links to the full list of Hague System contracting parties. Eligibility is established by nationality, residence/domicile, or real and effective industrial/commercial establishment within a contracting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where protection can be secured (scope of protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can secure protection within any contracting party, including member states of an intergovernmental organization party to the Hague Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you wish to protect a design in a jurisdiction that is not party to the Hague Agreement, you must file a national (or regional) application in that jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single international application / one language / one set of fees
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO's Hague System allows you to secure design protection simultaneously in multiple countries or regions through one international application, in one language with one set of fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no pre-requirement to file a national or regional design application in order to use the Hague System.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements and formality examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Once submitted, your application will be checked for compliance with form and content (formal requirements), including payment of the required fees. Examples of formal requirements include designation of contracting parties and quality of reproductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-payment or other non-compliance will result in an irregularity notice. Once application complies with formal requirements, WIPO records it in the International Register and issues a certificate of international registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularity notice and how to reply / timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: If an irregularity is found, WIPO will notify you and you have three months to fix those irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can reply to an irregularity letter directly through eHague. If you filed in paper format (directly with WIPO or via an IP office), you can upload a reply using the Hague System Document Upload service via Contact Hague; to use this service you need a WIPO Account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and flexible publication options
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO publishes your international registration in the International Designs Bulletin. By default this publication occurs twelve months after the international registration date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless you requested immediate publication or publication at a chosen time. Flexible publication options let you time release of your designs to fit your business strategy (e.g., request publication only when you are ready to unveil designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination by designated contracting parties
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication, the IP office of each designated contracting party may perform substantive examination checking whether designs comply with their domestic laws (for example: whether descriptions of reproductions are included, whether designs are novel, and whether they are not contrary to public morality or decency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every designated office examines; a list of contracting parties that have an examining office is provided (e.g., Canada, China, Japan, United States, etc.). Examination is carried out under the domestic law of each designated contracting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of protection (grounds, timing, and consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each designated contracting party has the right to refuse protection within its own territory, notifying WIPO within six (in some cases 12) months of the date of publication of the international registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no refusal is issued by a given IP office within the time limit, protection is deemed to be automatically granted in that jurisdiction under its established laws. A refusal by one office does not affect your international registration in other designated jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to a refusal and legal assistance limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If an office refuses protection you can contest the refusal according to the established domestic procedure at the IP office concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO offers online resources and you may raise specific enquiries through Contact Hague, but WIPO does not provide legal assistance; you should follow the domestic appeal/remedy procedures of the refusing office or consult local counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of protection and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial period of protection under the Hague System is five years. You can then renew your design twice, which guarantees you at least 15 years of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual contracting party legislation may allow for a longer duration of protection. The page points to resources to find out the maximum duration of protection in each contracting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing and making changes to international registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to keep your international registrations up-to-date; you may need to make changes such as changing ownership or representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can centrally manage and renew your registrations directly through WIPO. Contact Hague customer service for assistance; phone contact and online Contact Hague service are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search prior designs before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tip: Check what your competitors are doing by searching existing designs – virtual and print – before you file an international design application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested tools include the Global Design Database and Hague Express to help assess novelty and avoid conflicts before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred filing channel and supporting tools
rubrics_metrics.description: File your application directly with WIPO using eHague – the simplest and most efficient way to secure international design protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: eHague allows you to file and reply to irregularity letters directly. For paper filings, the Hague System Document Upload service exists for replies (requires a WIPO Account). Additional learning resources include webinars, digital information kit, and WIPO Academy distance learning courses.
